title: Living ashtpadi 19

segments.voice: Yesterday, what does go, and your line: kindness travels. Did you take the first step of a lasting kindness? Today we take the whole nineteenth ashtpadi off the page and into the house. Day five hundred thirteen.

Every home has one. The drawer. Dead batteries, a takeout menu from a restaurant that closed, three keys to locks nobody remembers, a phone charger for a phone from 2014, rubber bands that snap when you touch them. Nobody decided to keep any of it. It just collected, the way things do when nobody's looking. And every time you open that drawer looking for scissors, you have to dig. The nineteenth ashtpadi has spent three days on what stays behind and what goes along. Living it starts somewhere very small. Maybe with that drawer.
screen: `THE DRAWER EVERY HOME HAS.` → `IT JUST COLLECTED.` → `LIVING IT STARTS SMALL.`

segments.voice: Here's the nineteenth ashtpadi in one breath: the riches, youth and power we pile up stay behind; the Name we earn and the good we do go along. So how do people actually live that? Not, in Sikh teaching, by running away. The Gurus didn't ask Sikhs to become wandering monks with empty bowls. Guru Nanak spent his last years farming at Kartarpur, raising a family, running a community kitchen. Sikhs call that life grihasti, the householder's path, and they hold it up as a full spiritual life. So living light doesn't mean owning nothing. It means owning lightly: holding things with an open hand. One very concrete form of that is dasvandh, a tenth. Many Sikhs set aside a tenth of what they earn for the community: for langar, for a gurdwara's work, for someone in need. The tradition traces the practice to the time of the Gurus. It's not a fine or a tax. It's a habit of keeping your hand open, so that what passes through you can keep moving. And then there's the drawer. It may seem silly to link a junk drawer to a psalm, but Sukhmani works on the mind, and the mind is often cluttered in exactly that way: old grudges, worries about things that never happened, plans for a version of life you outgrew. Clearing a drawer won't clear all that. But it's practice. You learn to look at something, admit you're not using it, and let it go to someone who will. That's living light: not empty hands, open ones.
screen: `STAYS BEHIND, GOES ALONG.` · `NOT RUNNING AWAY: THE HOUSEHOLDER.` · `DASVANDH: A TENTH, GIVEN.` · `THE DRAWER: PRACTICE LETTING GO.` · then, large: `OPEN HANDS, NOT EMPTY ONES.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: clear out one drawer. If you can, go to it now. If you can't, picture it clearly. Take out one thing at a time and hold it for a breath. Ask: do I use this? Could someone else? Make three small piles: keep, give, throw away. Don't hurry, and don't judge yourself for what's in there. Just notice how the hand opens a little more each time. If you pray, you can say Waheguru as each thing goes. The bell holds the time.
Living ashtpadi 19. The householder's way: owning lightly, giving a tenth, and letting go of what you don't use so it can move on.
Your line: live light. Today, take the give pile somewhere it will be used: a donation box, a neighbor, a friend who needs a charger. Day five hundred thirteen.

howItsDone: Sikh teaching honors the householder's life rather than renunciation, and many Sikhs practice dasvandh, setting aside a tenth of their earnings for the community and those in need.

fork.setup: you've taken Sukhmani's nineteenth ashtpadi to heart. what does the Sikh tradition point you toward?

keep your life, but hold it with an open hand.
hold on tighter, since it all goes anyway.
fork.reveal: the Gurus chose the householder's path: farm, family, kitchen, and giving. living light means open hands, not empty ones.
